title: POC kickoff: performance charter & measurement plan - Northcape Analytics
summary: Kickoff for a 6-week POC to validate latency & throughput SLOs for Northcape's chat assistant. Reviewed traffic profile buckets, defined TTFT vs TPOT targets (p95/p99), agreed on benchmark methodology, and set timeline for an initial benchmark run and pilot. Action items: Redwood to share benchmark template + security pack; Northcape to provide sample prompts, traffic histograms, and pilot cluster credentials.
topics: POC success criteria and acceptance matrix
Traffic sizing: burst, steady, and tail behavior
next_steps: Redwood: send benchmark spreadsheet and traffic sample template
Northcape: upload representative prompt set (short/medium/long) and 30-day traffic histograms
Schedule lab benchmark run (lab slot week of Apr 17)
Security: Redwood to share SOC2 + KMS/SSO docs
Set recurring weekly syncs for pilot progress
action_items: Maya Chen: Share benchmark spreadsheet, measurement playbook, and a list of sample prompt buckets (due 2028-04-13)
Owen Park: Prepare a runnable load script and default traffic emulator for TTFT/TPOT sweeps (due 2028-04-15)
Lina Ortega: Provide 30-day traffic histograms and SLO priorities matrix (p95 vs p99 emphasis) (due 2028-04-14)
Samir Patel: Upload 200 representative prompts across short/med/long buckets, mark examples that use KV caching (due 2028-04-13)
Hannah Kim: Provide test VPC credentials and list of allowed CIDRs for pilot lab (due 2028-04-16)
transcript: [00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. We have Owen from SE here as well. Lina, Samir, Hannah, thanks for carving time.
[00:12] Lina: Thanks Maya. Quick note, it's 11am our side. We put together a short agenda in the invite; main goal is to lock down success criteria and measurement plan for the POC.

[00:24] Owen: Great. I'll go high-level on how we think about TTFT vs TPOT and then suggest a benchmark sequence. Quick question up front: is Northcape prioritizing first-response latency (user perceived start) or total per-token cost/latency under sustained throughput?

[00:40] Samir: For our chat assistant the UX team cares about time-to-first-token — if the user waits more than ~200ms they notice. But the ops team also worries about steady-state per-token cost because we expect millions of tokens per month. So really both, but prioritize TTFT for user-facing flows and TPOT for background generation jobs.

[00:59] Maya: Perfect, that's a common tradeoff. For the POC we'll split acceptance into two axes: TTFT SLOs and TPOT SLOs, with sample-based measurement and traffic-shapings. Owen, can you outline the targets we typically test to get meaningful pass/fail criteria?

[01:12] Owen: Sure. Based on similar customers we propose initial targets: TTFT p95 at 120ms, p99 at 280ms for short dialog prompts (~<64 tokens). For long prompts the p95 naturally increases; we'll define buckets. For TPOT (per-token) we aim p95 8-12ms, p99 <25ms under steady load depending on model size and quantization. These are starting points — we expect to tune with your traffic profile.
[01:38] Lina: That p99 for TTFT seems tight. Do those numbers assume Dedicated GPU pools or hosted multi-tenant?

[01:47] Owen: Good call — those are realistic on Redwood Dedicated with 1:1 or 2:1 GPU sharing and optimized kernels. On hosted we see more variance; if you need strict p99s we recommend Dedicated or private deployment with pinned model variant. We'll capture both in the benchmark.

[02:05] Hannah: Also curious about warm vs cold cache. Our flows have a lot of repeated prefixes and we rely on KV caching in prod; so warm-start TTFT should be much lower than cold-start. Can we test both?

[02:18] Owen: Absolutely. Our measurement plan includes three cache states: cold (no KV), warm (prefetch with cache hits ~60-80%), and steady-state with prefix reuse. We'll parameterize the bench script to toggle cache-hit rates.
[02:32] Samir: How do you collect p95/p99? Are you instrumenting at the client side or at the host? We need to ensure numbers are comparable to our in-app telemetry.

[02:42] Maya: We recommend collecting both: client-side synthetic probes to measure end-to-end TTFT and host-side traces (Redwood console traces) for breakdowns — parse model compute vs queueing vs network. We'll align our clocks and provide a CSV export so you can reconcile with your telemetry.
[02:57] Lina: Ok. We also need to define acceptance matrix. For example if TTFT p95 is met but p99 is blown during bursts, is that a fail?

[03:08] Owen: We'll propose a weighted acceptance matrix: core UX flows (80% of traffic) must meet TTFT p95 threshold, p99 can have a small tolerated failure rate if you have fallback logic. For critical flows we can require hard p99 limits. We'll draft that in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:26] Maya: I'll add that to the success criteria section. Next, traffic profile. Hannah, can you describe today's traffic in terms of qps and burstiness?

[03:36] Hannah: Sure. Steady is about 20 reqs/sec for the assistant, with spikes up to 200 reqs/sec for short bursts (approx 2-3 minutes) during releases. Token lengths: 60% short (<64), 30% medium (64-256), 10% long (>256). KV cache hit roughly 55% on average.

[03:54] Owen: That's helpful. For benching we'll create three traffic shapes: steady (20 qps), burst (200 qps for 3 minutes), and ramp (0 to 200 over 10 minutes). We'll run each shape across the prompt buckets and report TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99 plus error rates.
[04:10] Samir: Error rates — do you include model fallbacks? In production we want automatic fallback to a smaller model if latency jumps.

[04:18] Owen: Yes, we can run experiments with Redwood routing policies: primary model vs fallback. We'll measure the graceful degradation behavior and tail impact. We'll also capture cost delta per fallback event.
[04:29] Lina: On security/compliance — we need SOC2 docs, key management info, and audit logs for the pilot. Also SSO for Redwood console.

[04:38] Maya: We'll send our security pack (SOC2 report, encryption at rest/TLS, KMS options, SSO/SAML config) after the call. We'll also note that Private deployment with customer-managed KMS is an option for the pilot if needed.
[04:49] Hannah: For the lab bench we prefer VPC peering to our staging VPC rather than public egress. Is that supported for the pilot?

[04:58] Owen: Yes — for Private/Dedicated we can do VPC peering or private endpoints. For the hosted lab we can use an isolated egress allowed CIDR list. We'll capture the exact options in the runbook.
[05:10] Samir: Measurement specifics: what's the sample size to compute stable p99 metrics? We had noisy p99s last time with 100 samples.

[05:18] Owen: For p99 stability we like at least several thousand samples per bucket; in practice 2,000–10,000 requests per bucket depending on variance. We'll design runs to accumulate sufficient samples over repeat runs and produce confidence intervals.
[05:31] Lina: That will take time — how long will benchmarking take end-to-end?

[05:36] Maya: Proposed discovery timeline: week 1 (this week) — gather artifacts and schedule lab; week 2 — run initial benchmark including cold/warm/steady shapes; week 3 — iterate with tuning (batching, quantization) and run targeted runs; week 4 — pilot handoff and start a 2-week pilot in your staging with live-ish traffic. So roughly 4–6 weeks to sign off depending on tuning needs.
[05:57] Hannah: Sounds good. Can you talk about where quantization and kernel selection come into the benchmarks? We use an MPT-style open model and want to compare 8-bit quantized vs fp16.

[06:08] Owen: We'll include model variants: fp16 baseline, 8-bit quantized, and a trimmed smaller model for fallback. The runtime will select kernels per sequence length; we'll capture per-token latency breakdown. We'll also show cost delta per token across variants so you can weigh quality vs cost.
[06:25] Samir: For quality regression we also need to run a small eval set — we want to ensure quantized model doesn't regress on the top 10 intents.

[06:33] Maya: Good point — include a short quality suite of ~200 eval prompts to run after each variant change; we'll include BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics and some intent-level checks, plus a manual spot check.

[06:45] Lina: For acceptance criteria: propose we require TTFT p95 met for short and medium buckets, TPOT p95 met for steady-state. Allow p99 excursions but capped at X% of requests — can you propose exact numbers in the matrix?

[06:58] Owen: We'll propose a matrix where critical flows must meet p95 thresholds and p99 must be less than 1.5x the p95 for critical flows, otherwise require mitigation. Non-critical flows can accept 2x p95. We'll write this formally in the spreadsheet.

[07:12] Maya: Alright. Let's talk about telemetry and where we measure. We'll provide a runbook with the exact events to capture (request_sent, first_token, last_token, tokens_emitted, model_variant, KV_cache_hit). That should map to your in-app events.
[07:28] Hannah: Good. Also need to know what logging retention and cost look like if we capture per-token traces for a month.
[07:35] Owen: We'll show estimated storage and cost for 30-day retention in the console add-on. And for the POC we can keep sampling-level traces only for benchmark runs to limit cost.
[07:46] Lina: One more thing — we'd like to see a guardrail playbook: if TPOT or TTFT degrades in production what should be the immediate runbook?

[07:55] Maya: We'll include a runbook with prioritized mitigations: 1) Redirect to warm caches / increase batch size, 2) Route to smaller model variant, 3) Temporarily increase capacity (burst pool), 4) Apply traffic shaping for non-critical flows. We'll include SRE runbooks with commands for each.
[08:11] Samir: On the topic of traffic shaping — do you support token-based rate limits or only request-based? Our long prompts can be heavy.
[08:18] Owen: Both. You can set per-route token budgets and per-API key limits. We'll include example configs for your long-prompt flows.

[08:28] Lina: Okay — to summarize, we need the benchmark template, security docs, sample prompts, traffic histograms, and VPC info. Then Redwood runs lab bench week of Apr 17, we iterate, and start a 2-week staging pilot. Is that accurate?
[08:42] Maya: Yes. I'll put those dates in the next steps. Anything else we're missing?
[08:48] Hannah: Can you also include a cost sensitivity analysis? We want an estimate of $/million tokens for each model variant and baseline configuration.
[08:55] Owen: We'll include a cost breakdown by per-token compute + networking + caching delta across variants. That will be in the benchmark report.
[09:03] Lina: Great. One concern: our CISO may push for private deployment. Can the POC run as private connect with our KMS?

[09:11] Maya: Yes — we can spin a Private pilot with your KMS and a customer-managed VPC but that requires slightly longer setup (usually an extra week). We'll list both options and tradeoffs in the plan.
[09:23] Samir: For the actual benchmark runs, can we get raw logs and the console-time series? We want to plug it into our observability stack.
[09:30] Owen: We'll provide CSV exports of raw measurements and a Grafana/Prometheus-compatible metrics stream for the pilot. That will allow you to overlay with your traces.

[09:40] Maya: Alright, we've hit most items. I'll read back the action items — Maya send bench spreadsheet, Owen load scripts, Lina provide traffic histograms, Samir provide prompts, Hannah provide VPC creds. We'll aim for an initial lab run week of Apr 17 and send security pack today.
[09:56] Lina: Sounds good, thanks all. Quick note: we'll prioritize TTFT for the web chat product, but want the cost analysis to decide long-term whether to go Dedicated or hosted.
[10:07] Maya: Perfect — we'll make sure both Hosted and Dedicated scenarios are benchmarked. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and I'll drop the spreadsheet and runbook links.
[10:18] Samir: One last question — for the p99 numbers, how do you handle network jitter from client-side? We saw spikes last-minute that skewed p99.

[10:25] Owen: We'll run both synthetic probes colocated in the lab and also your real-client probes. For reconciliation we'll run server-side-only latency and client+network traces and indicate the delta.
[10:35] Hannah: Okay, thanks. We'll wait for the materials and schedule.
[10:40] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the bench slot. Meeting adjourned.
[10:45] (call ended)
